hints: Notice the observed frequency $3.0\text{ Hz}$ is greater than the source frequency $2.0\text{ Hz}$ - decide whether the wavefronts reaching the man must be compressed or stretched.
Recall the moving-source Doppler relation $f_o = f_s v / (v - v_s)$ for motion towards the observer, where $v = 1.5\text{ m s}^{-1}$ is the water-wave speed.
Substitute $f_o = 3.0\text{ Hz}$ and $f_s = 2.0\text{ Hz}$ and solve for $v_s$, then check which speed and direction pair matches that value.
walkthrough: Observed frequency is higher than source frequency: $3.0\text{ Hz} > 2.0\text{ Hz}$. Higher frequency means shorter observed wavelength at the man, so the boat must be moving directly towards the man to catch up with its own wavefronts.
For a source moving towards a stationary observer, use $f_o = f_s \times v / (v - v_s)$, where $v = 1.5\text{ m s}^{-1}$ is the wave speed and $v_s$ is the source speed.
Solve: $4.5 - 3.0v_s = 3.0$, so $3.0v_s = 1.5$ and $v_s = 0.50\text{ m s}^{-1}$. Units remain $\text{m s}^{-1}$ as required.
Thus the possible motion is $0.50\text{ m s}^{-1}$ directly towards the man. This is option B.

options.A: Moving away would stretch the observed wavelength and give $f_o < 2.0\text{ Hz}$, so it cannot explain the observed $3.0\text{ Hz}$.
options.B: Moving towards the man at $0.50\text{ m s}^{-1}$ shortens the observed wavelength enough to raise $2.0\text{ Hz}$ to $3.0\text{ Hz}$.
options.C: Moving away would lower the observed frequency, and $0.75\text{ m s}^{-1}$ does not satisfy the Doppler equation for $3.0\text{ Hz}$.
options.D: Motion towards the man is correct for an increase in frequency, but $0.75\text{ m s}^{-1}$ would give $f_o = 4.0\text{ Hz}$, not $3.0\text{ Hz}$.
